extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media critics, and readers concerned with editorial ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and producing magazine/profile interviews where AI is used to generate a subject's replies or to stand in for access to a celebrity. Focus is on editorial decisions, ethics, taste, and journalistic purpose when AI is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish fabricated interviews; spike if no access
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic idea that you wouldn’t just spike the whole piece due to scheduling issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is unavailable, do not manufacture an entire interview. The piece criticizes running a wholly made-up 'AI interview' rather than cancelling or postponing; spiking the piece is a legitimate editorial option when genuine access is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting AI-generated replies as the subject's authentic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine took a bunch of Mackenyu’s old interview answers, ran them through an AI, and then pelted the language model with their own questions, generating a laundry list of banal, cookie cutter 'answers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not imply that AI-generated text is the subject speaking. If AI is used, clearly disclose its role and avoid claiming authenticity. Editorial oversight must prevent misrepresentation of authorship/voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask interesting, substantive questions (don't rely on AI to compensate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent belief that Esquire Singapore was incapable of coming up with questions interesting enough to baffle a half-assed Claude drone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and writers should craft thoughtful questions that can produce insight; relying on AI to rescue weak questioning leads to banal, cookie-cutter answers and indicates poor preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use AI to speculate on sensitive personal topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial myopia involved in reading the 'AI Mackenyu' speculate on the 29-year-old’s relationship to the legacy of his late father, acclaimed martial arts actor Sonny Chiba, and not thinking, 'Hey, even for an inherently ghoulish concept, this should probably be cut.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prompting or publishing AI speculation about a subject's private or potentially traumatic family relationships, grief, or legacy without explicit consent and careful editorial consideration; such speculation is unethical and tasteless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ghoulishness and desperate stunts in place of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Facing deadlines and no apparent barriers of taste, Esquire Singapore made an 'AI copy'... The resulting piece is a staggering success in the field of journalistic and editorial failure... a ghoulish little desperation play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute sensational or grotesque stunt pieces for genuine reporting. Editorial teams should evaluate whether a concept is tasteful or merely desperate attention-seeking and cut material that reduces the subject to a spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hide ethical lapses behind artistic-framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Esquire Singapore posits this as some sort of artistic expression on the unknowability of celebrity and the inherent distance of interviewing famous people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing a fabrication as 'art' or an 'experiment' does not absolve ethical or journalistic failures. Transparency about methods and justification is required; artistic rationale should not be used to excuse deception or low effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews should shed new light on the subject's work and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' actual job involves sometimes figuring out how to talk to very well-known people about their lives and careers in ways that shed new light on their work and what it means to us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary evaluative criterion for a profile/interview is whether it offers genuine insight or illumination about the subject's career, work, or cultural significance; filler or recycled platitudes fail this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience and fanbase reactions when making editorial choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The article was actually published... (Mackenyu’s extremely vocal fanbase is not happy, apparently.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should anticipate and weigh how fans and the subject's community will react to fabricated or ethically dubious pieces; failing to do so can damage credibility and relationships with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise editorial judgment to cut problematic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial myopia... and not thinking, 'Hey, even for an inherently ghoulish concept, this should probably be cut.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must intervene to remove or revise content that crosses ethical/taste lines or that misrepresents the subject, rather than allowing novelty or deadline pressure to justify publishing harmful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: If using AI, ensure outputs are quality-controlled and not banal
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating a laundry list of banal, cookie cutter 'answers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When AI is part of the process, apply rigorous editorial quality control: vet outputs for insight, originality, and sensitivity; rework, contextualize, or discard AI-generated material that is clichéd or shallow.
